questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, which of the following correctly defines the job of the OSI model's Transport layer (Layer 4)?
options: Breaks data into segments, adds port numbers, and handles reliability — the job TCP and UDP do
Adds logical IP addressing and routes between networks
Adds physical MAC addressing for the local network segment
Formats, encrypts, and compresses data for the application
Opens, manages, and closes a conversation between two hosts
The actual electrical signal, light, or radio wave carrying the data
questions.explain: Lesson 1's table assigns each OSI layer one job: Transport (Layer 4) breaks data into segments, adds port numbers, and handles reliability — that's exactly what TCP and UDP do. Network (Layer 3) handles IP addressing and routing, and Data Link (Layer 2) handles MAC addressing, which is why confusing those two with Transport is the classic mix-up.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes the Network layer (Layer 3), not the Transport layer — IP addressing and routing between networks is specifically what Lesson 1's table assigns to Layer 3, one layer below Transport. Mixing up 'adds port numbers' (Transport) with 'adds IP addresses and routes' (Network) is exactly the kind of layer confusion the OSI model's one-job-per-layer structure is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, put these troubleshooting checks in the correct bottom-up order a network engineer would actually use.
items: Physical — is the cable/radio link actually up?
Data Link — is the switch port forwarding frames?
Network — does the device have a valid, routable IP?
Transport — is the right port open and reachable?
Application — only now does 'the app is broken' mean anything
questions.explain: Lesson 1 is explicit that troubleshooting goes bottom-up: confirm the cable is plugged in and the link light is on before chasing an application error, because nothing above a broken lower layer can possibly work, no matter how correct it is.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 3's worked example, the subnet 192.168.1.0/27 has 5 host bits, so 2^5 - 2 = ________ usable host addresses.
questions.explain: A /27 leaves 32 - 27 = 5 host bits, giving 2^5 = 32 total addresses. Subtracting the 2 reserved addresses (the network address and the broadcast address) leaves 30 usable host addresses — exactly Lesson 3's worked example.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about TCP and UDP, per Lesson 2.
options: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before any real data flows
UDP guarantees ordered, reliable delivery of every packet, the same as TCP
DNS lookups, video streaming, and online gaming typically use UDP because speed matters more than a delivery guarantee
TCP/IP's Application layer collapses OSI's Application, Presentation, and Session layers into one
The three-way handshake belongs to UDP, not TCP
questions.explain: TCP's three-way handshake establishes a connection before data flows, and TCP/IP's Application layer really does fold OSI's top three layers together. UDP is the opposite of 'guarantees ordered, reliable delivery' — that's TCP's job — which is exactly why UDP fits DNS lookups, streaming, and gaming, where a late retransmit is worse than a dropped packet.

questions.prompt: A router's routing table has two entries that both could match a packet destined for 192.168.20.20: the connected route 192.168.20.0/24 and the default route 0.0.0.0/0. Per Lesson 6, which entry does the router actually use, and why?
options: 192.168.20.0/24 — the router always uses the longest prefix match, the most specific entry that matches
0.0.0.0/0 — the default route always takes priority over any more specific entry
Both — the router splits the traffic evenly between the two matching routes
Neither — two matching entries mean the packet is dropped as unroutable
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is explicit that for every packet, a router finds the most specific matching entry — the longest prefix match — and forwards according to that. The default route only catches traffic when nothing more specific matches, which is why it's called the 'gateway of last resort,' not the first choice.

questions.prompt: Match each DNS record type from Lesson 7 to what it actually does.
right: Maps a name directly to an IPv4 address
An alias that points one name to another name, not directly to an address
Mail exchange — which mail server handles email for a domain, and in what priority order
Free-form text, commonly used for domain ownership verification and anti-spoofing records
questions.explain: Lesson 7 lays out each record type's actual job: A maps straight to an IPv4 address, CNAME is an alias pointing to another name (which the resolver must keep following until it hits an A/AAAA record), MX names the mail server and its priority, and TXT holds free-form text like SPF/DKIM verification.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 8, DHCP's four-step exchange — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — is abbreviated ________.
questions.explain: DORA is the acronym Lesson 8 says is worth memorizing cold: Discover (client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER), Offer (server replies DHCPOFFER), Request (client sends DHCPREQUEST), Acknowledge (server confirms with DHCPACK).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about NAT and firewalls, per Lesson 9.
options: PAT (Port Address Translation) lets every device behind a router share one public IP address, distinguished by port
A stateful firewall automatically allows the reply to an outbound request it already approved, without a separate rule
A stateless firewall needs explicit rules for both the outbound request and its matching inbound reply
Private IP ranges like 192.168.0.0/16 are routable directly on the public internet
ACL rules are evaluated in order, and the first matching rule wins
questions.explain: PAT is the NAT variant nearly every home router runs, distinguishing shared-address connections by port. A stateful firewall remembers approved outbound connections and auto-allows the reply, while a stateless firewall has no such memory and needs explicit rules both ways. ACL rules are read top to bottom with first-match-wins. Private IP ranges are specifically reserved so they're never routed on the public internet — the opposite of the false statement.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes using `sudo` from simply logging in directly as the root user?
options: sudo lets an authorized regular user run a single command with root privileges after re-entering their own password, with that action logged; logging in directly as root bypasses that per-command authorization and audit trail
sudo permanently elevates a user account to root, identical to changing that account's UID to 0
Logging in directly as root automatically logs every command run, while sudo logs nothing
sudo and logging in directly as root are functionally identical — the only difference is which prompt is shown
questions.explain: Lesson 13 explains that sudo lets an authorized user run one command with root privileges, requires re-entering their own password, and logs the action — which is exactly why production servers let everyone use their own account plus sudo instead of logging in directly as root, giving an audit trail of who ran what.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes a permanent account change, not sudo — sudo grants root privileges for a single command, one at a time, and the user's account is never actually changed to UID 0. Treating sudo as a permanent elevation rather than a per-command, logged exception is exactly the misunderstanding Lesson 13 is built to correct.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 13, the command ________ 755 deploy.sh sets owner=rwx, group=r-x, and other=r-x.
questions.explain: chmod changes permission bits, and 755 in octal breaks down to owner=7 (rwx), group=5 (r-x), other=5 (r-x) — exactly the permission set Lesson 13 says you'll see on nearly every executable script and web server file.

questions.prompt: Match each directory from Lesson 11's Filesystem Hierarchy Standard to what actually lives there.
right: System-wide configuration files that nearly every service reads its settings from
Where the system and most services write their log files by default
Temporary files any user or process can write to, routinely wiped on reboot
questions.explain: The FHS gives every top-level directory a consistent job across distros: /etc holds configuration, /var/log holds logs, /home holds user directories, and /tmp holds temporary files that are routinely cleared on reboot — which is exactly what lets you navigate an unfamiliar server with confidence.

questions.prompt: You SSH into an unfamiliar cloud VM and run `apt install curl`, which fails with 'command not found.' Per Lesson 14, what does this most likely tell you, and what would you try instead?
options: The VM is likely running a RHEL-family or Amazon Linux distro rather than Debian/Ubuntu, so `dnf install curl` (or `yum install curl`) is the right command to try instead
The VM has no internet connection, so no package manager command will work until connectivity is restored
curl does not exist as an installable package on any Linux distro
The VM's root filesystem is corrupted and needs to be reinstalled
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that apt belongs to the Debian/Ubuntu family, while RHEL, CentOS, Fedora, and Amazon Linux use yum/dnf instead — the two command sets differ even though the underlying tasks (refresh, install, remove, search) are the same shape. A missing `apt` command points at the distro family, not connectivity or disk corruption.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes SIGTERM from SIGKILL?
options: SIGTERM is a polite request that lets a well-behaved process clean up and exit on its own terms; SIGKILL is an unconditional kill with no chance to clean up
SIGTERM is an unconditional kill that a process cannot ignore; SIGKILL is a polite request the process can choose to ignore
Both signals behave identically; SIGKILL is just a newer alias for SIGTERM
SIGTERM only works on services managed by systemd, while SIGKILL works on any process
SIGKILL is always sent before SIGTERM in a normal shutdown sequence
questions.explain: Lesson 15 defines SIGTERM (signal 15) as a polite request a well-behaved process catches and reacts to by cleaning up before exiting, and SIGKILL (signal 9) as an unconditional kill with no chance to clean up — which is exactly why you always try plain `kill` before reaching for `kill -9`.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two signals' behavior entirely backwards — it's SIGTERM that can be caught and gracefully handled, and SIGKILL that is the unconditional, un-ignorable kill. Reversing which signal is the polite request and which is the forced termination is exactly the mix-up Lesson 15 warns against, since killing a database with SIGKILL instead of SIGTERM can leave corrupted files behind.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, put these three troubleshooting steps in the order an admin should actually run them when a web service appears to be down.
items: systemctl status <service> — is it even running?
journalctl -u <service> -n 50 — what has the service itself logged recently?
tail -f /var/log/syslog — is the wider system reporting anything related?
questions.explain: Lesson 17's real troubleshooting workflow moves from specific to broad: check the service's own status first, then its own recent log entries, and only then the wider system log — most problems show up in the first two steps, and the third is only needed when the service itself looks healthy but something underneath (disk, memory, network) isn't.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 18, the first line of every bash script (e.g. #!/bin/bash), which tells the system which program should interpret the rest of the file, is called the ________.
questions.explain: The shebang (`#!` followed by the interpreter's path) is what tells the system a file full of commands should specifically be run by bash — without it, the system has no reliable way to know how to execute the script.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SSH key-based authentication, per Lesson 16.
options: The private key half of an SSH key pair should never leave your own machine
The public key needs to be placed in a file called authorized_keys inside ~/.ssh on the server
ssh-keygen generates only a public key; the matching private key must be created with a separate command
SSH listens on port 22 by default
Revoking someone's key-based access requires resetting a shared password for every other user
questions.explain: Lesson 16 is specific that ssh-keygen generates both halves of the pair at once, the private key stays on your machine, the public key goes into the server's authorized_keys file, and SSH defaults to port 22. Revoking access is one line deleted from authorized_keys, not a password reset for anyone else.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor from a Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor?
options: A Type 1 hypervisor installs directly on the physical hardware with no host OS underneath, like VMware ESXi or KVM; a Type 2 hypervisor installs as an application on top of a regular host OS, like VirtualBox
A Type 2 hypervisor installs directly on hardware with no host OS, while a Type 1 hypervisor runs as an application inside Windows or macOS
Type 1 hypervisors are used only for development and testing, never in production
There is no real technical difference between the two; the numbering only reflects release order
questions.explain: Lesson 19 defines Type 1 as installing directly on hardware with no host OS competing for resources (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, Xen), which is why every production datacenter and public cloud runs it. Type 2 installs as an ordinary application on top of a host OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation), which is why it's used for development and testing, not production.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses the two definitions entirely — it's Type 1 that has no host OS underneath, and Type 2 that runs as an application on top of one. Swapping which type is bare-metal and which is hosted is precisely the confusion Lesson 19 is built to prevent, since it also reverses which type is actually safe to run in production.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about containers vs. virtual machines, per Lesson 21.
options: A container shares the host's existing kernel instead of running its own full guest OS
Namespaces give each container its own isolated view of PIDs, network interfaces, and mount points
cgroups limit how much CPU, memory, and I/O each container is allowed to consume
Containers typically take thirty seconds to a couple of minutes to start, the same as a VM
Most production environments choose only containers or only VMs, never both together
questions.explain: A container's defining trait is sharing the host kernel rather than booting its own OS, isolated by namespaces (process/network/mount views) and limited by cgroups (resource caps). That shared-kernel model is exactly why containers start in well under a second, not the thirty-seconds-to-minutes a VM's full OS boot takes — and Lesson 21 notes most production environments actually run both together, containers on top of VMs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 22, AWS's lightweight, KVM-based hypervisor platform, combined with dedicated offload hardware for networking, storage, and security, is called ________.
questions.explain: Nitro is AWS's own hypervisor platform — a lightweight, KVM-based hypervisor plus dedicated Nitro Cards that offload networking, storage, and security away from the main CPU, so most of a physical server's compute goes to customer VMs instead of virtualization overhead.

questions.prompt: A hypervisor host has 64 GB of physical RAM but is running VMs whose combined assigned RAM totals 96 GB. Per Lesson 20, what is this technique called, and why does it typically work without every VM running out of memory at once?
options: Memory overcommit — it relies on not every VM using its full allocation at the same instant, and can reclaim unused RAM from one VM with techniques like memory ballooning
Memory virtualization failure — this configuration always crashes every VM on the host immediately
Thin provisioning — a storage-only technique that has nothing to do with RAM allocation
Hardware-assisted virtualization — a CPU feature unrelated to how much RAM is assigned
questions.explain: Lesson 20 names this memory overcommit: assigning VMs more total virtual RAM than the host physically has, which works because not every VM uses its full allocation simultaneously, and memory ballooning lets the hypervisor reclaim unused RAM from one VM to hand to another that needs it.

questions.prompt: Match each cloud service model from Lesson 23 to what it actually means, with its real example.
right: Provider manages hardware and virtualization; you manage the OS up — e.g. AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines
Provider manages the OS and runtime too; you manage your app and data — e.g. Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk
Provider manages the entire stack; you just use the application — e.g. Microsoft 365, Salesforce
The virtualization layer that carves physical hardware into isolated virtual machines
questions.explain: Lesson 23's layer-by-layer breakdown shows the provider/customer line sliding upward from IaaS to SaaS: IaaS leaves the OS up to you, PaaS takes the OS and runtime off your plate, and SaaS manages the entire application — with the hypervisor as the virtualization layer underneath all three.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes 'security OF the cloud' from 'security IN the cloud'?
options: Security OF the cloud is always the provider's job — physical datacenters, host hardware, and the hypervisor; security IN the cloud is the customer's job — their data, identity and access management, and the configuration they control
Security OF the cloud is the customer's job, while security IN the cloud is always the provider's job
Both terms describe the exact same set of responsibilities, just phrased differently by AWS versus Azure
Security OF the cloud only applies to SaaS products, and security IN the cloud only applies to IaaS products
questions.explain: Lesson 24 draws the line squarely: the provider always owns security OF the cloud (physical security, host hardware, the hypervisor), while the customer always owns security IN the cloud (their data, IAM, and the configuration they're given) — a line that doesn't move, even as the specific tasks on each side shift between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two responsibilities entirely — the provider never hands physical datacenter and hypervisor security to the customer, and the customer never hands their own data and access control off to the provider. Reversing which side owns which half of the split is exactly the mistake that leads to blaming a provider for a customer-side misconfiguration like a leaked access key.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about public, private, and hybrid cloud, per Lesson 25.
options: Public cloud is multi-tenant: the same physical datacenters and hardware serve many different customers at once
Private cloud means infrastructure dedicated to a single organization, whether on-premises or hosted
Hybrid cloud just means using more than one cloud vendor's tools, with no actual network connection required between them
Azure ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN are real examples of the private, dedicated link a hybrid setup relies on
Compliance and data-residency requirements are a real business reason a company might choose hybrid cloud
questions.explain: Lesson 25 defines public cloud as multi-tenant shared infrastructure and private cloud as dedicated infrastructure for one organization. Hybrid cloud is specifically a real, connected mix — on-premises and public cloud linked over something like ExpressRoute or a site-to-site VPN — not just using multiple vendors with no connection, and compliance/data-residency is one of the concrete business reasons the lesson gives for choosing it.

questions.prompt: An application runs two virtual machines, both placed in us-east-1a. Per Lesson 26, why doesn't this protect the application from a datacenter outage, even with two VMs instead of one?
options: Both VMs are in the same Availability Zone, so a power or network failure at that one facility takes down both of them at once — real protection requires spreading VMs across multiple AZs
us-east-1a is not a real AWS Availability Zone name
Having two VMs in the same AZ automatically doubles that facility's physical power redundancy
This setup only fails if the VMs are also placed in different AWS regions
questions.explain: Lesson 26 is explicit that an AZ is one physically separate datacenter with its own independent power and networking — putting both VMs in the same AZ means a single facility failure takes both down together. The actual protection comes from spreading VMs across two or three AZs within a region, so a load balancer can shift traffic to the AZs still healthy.

questions.prompt: A subnet's route table has no route pointing to an internet gateway. Per Lesson 28, what does that make the subnet, and what kind of resource would typically be placed inside it?
options: A private subnet — nothing inside it can reach the internet directly, making it the right place for something like a database layer that should never be exposed
A public subnet — the absence of a route automatically means all traffic is allowed out to the internet by default
An unusable subnet — a subnet without an internet gateway route cannot host any resources at all
This has no effect on whether the subnet is public or private; that is determined only by its security group
questions.explain: Lesson 28 defines a subnet's public/private status entirely by its route table: a route sending unmatched traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to an internet gateway makes it public, and the absence of that route makes it private — exactly where you'd put a database layer that should never be exposed directly to the internet.

questions.prompt: Match each cloud concept from Chapter 7 to what it actually is.
right: Flat, API-accessed storage for whole objects, e.g. AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage — ideal for backups and static files
Raw storage blocks attached to a single VM like a hard drive, e.g. AWS EBS or Azure Managed Disks
A shared, hierarchical filesystem multiple VMs can mount at once, e.g. AWS EFS or Azure Files
Distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances for availability and scale
questions.explain: Lesson 30 draws a clean line between the three storage types by what each is built for — object storage for unstructured, API-accessed data; block storage for a single VM's fast disk; file storage for a filesystem multiple VMs share — and Lesson 29 defines the load balancer that often sits in front of those shared application servers.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 29, AWS's Layer 7 load balancer, which can read the URL path and route /api/* and /images/* to different backend pools, is called the ________.
questions.explain: The Application Load Balancer (ALB) is Lesson 29's real example of Layer 7, application-aware load balancing — it reads the actual HTTP request, including the URL path, and routes accordingly, unlike the Network Load Balancer (NLB), which only sees IP and port.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 31's end-to-end lab, put these steps for provisioning and connecting to a new Linux VM in the correct order.
items: Pick the correct subnet for the VM based on whether it needs to be public-facing
Generate an SSH key pair on your own machine before the VM exists
Create the VM with the public key attached and an NSG inbound rule scoped to a known IP range
Connect to the VM using the matching private key
Run first-login checks: systemctl status sshd, apt update/upgrade, and review /var/log/auth.log
questions.explain: Lesson 31 walks the lab in exactly this order: the subnet decision comes first since it determines routing and the security group, the SSH key pair is generated before the VM exists so the public key can be installed at creation, the VM and its locked-down NSG rule come next, then the connection, and only after a short first-login checklist is the VM considered genuinely ready.

questions.prompt: On the new Briarcliff VM in Lesson 32, /var/log/auth.log showed no login attempts at all — not failed attempts, none. Why does that specific detail point at the network/NSG layer rather than at sshd or user authentication?
options: If SSH traffic had actually reached the VM and failed to authenticate, auth.log would show those failed attempts; a completely empty log means the traffic never arrived at the VM at all, which points at the NSG rule silently dropping it before it ever reached sshd
auth.log only records successful logins, so an empty log is expected and tells you nothing either way
An empty auth.log always means the VM's disk is full and can no longer write new log entries
sshd writes exclusively to journalctl and never to auth.log, so this detail is irrelevant to the diagnosis
questions.explain: Lesson 32's diagnosis hinges on exactly this: an empty auth.log, with zero attempts logged, means traffic never arrived at sshd to be evaluated in the first place — if it had arrived and failed, there would be failed-attempt entries. That absence of evidence pointed squarely at the NSG's stale source-IP range silently dropping the traffic, not at sshd or the OS.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how the Lesson 32 capstone incident was actually diagnosed and fixed.
options: Confirming the VM's power state first ruled out the simplest explanation before checking networking or the OS
The NSG's Allow-SSH rule itself had not changed, but the office's actual public IP range had moved to a new block
Checking the subnet's effective routes confirmed the problem was not a bad user-defined route overriding the default internet path
The root cause required reinstalling the VM's operating system
Checking broad infrastructure layers before narrower ones — network, then cloud config, then OS — is the deliberate order this course teaches
questions.explain: Lesson 32 checks the VM's running state first (ruling out the simplest failure), finds the NSG rule unchanged but pointed at a stale office IP range, confirms the route table was untouched, and fixes it with a one-line update to the rule's source address — no reinstall needed. That broad-to-narrow order (network, then cloud config, then OS) is explicitly the habit the lesson says carries into the rest of the path.
